goal: Implement the notes-cli milestone by choosing how note data is persisted, so the placeholder CLI can be replaced with working note storage.
question: Select the storage backend that notes-cli will use to persist note data on the user's local machine, given that the tool is a single-user, fully offline CLI with only one process touching the data at a time and no storage code written yet.
known_constraints: The CLI runs entirely offline on the user's own machine; no network access is required or desired (README.md).
Only one process touches the data at a time; single user (README.md).
The project currently declares zero runtime dependencies (pyproject.toml: dependencies = []).
Implementation language is Python (requires-python >=3.10); the console script `notes` maps to `notes.cli:main` (pyproject.toml).
Choosing the storage backend blocks the current milestone (TODO in src/notes/cli.py).
evidence: README.md states notes-cli is a single-user note-taking CLI that runs entirely offline on the user's own machine and that no network access is required or desired.
README.md states only one process touches the data at a time.
pyproject.toml declares an empty runtime dependency list (`dependencies = []`), requires Python >=3.10, and exposes the console script `notes = notes.cli:main` with a setuptools build backend.
src/notes/cli.py contains only a placeholder `main()` that prints 'notes-cli: no storage backend yet' and carries the TODO 'choose storage backend (this decision blocks the milestone)'.

Repository layout: the only source files are src/notes/__init__.py (empty) and src/notes/cli.py; there is no note data model, no schema, no tests, no existing storage code, and no data files anywhere in the repository.
The interpreter on this machine is Python 3.14.7, which satisfies requires-python >=3.10 (source: `python3 --version`).

The Python standard library on this machine provides `sqlite3` (SQLite 3.53.4), `json`, and `pathlib`, so every option under consideration can be implemented without third-party packages (source: `import sqlite3, json, pathlib` in the local interpreter).

alternatives.name: Single JSON file
alternatives.description: Persist all notes as one JSON document (for example notes.json in a user data directory) that is read into memory on startup and rewritten on each change.
advantages: Human-readable format the user can inspect, back up, or edit with any text editor.
Uses only the standard-library `json` module, keeping the project at zero runtime dependencies.
Small amount of straightforward code: load, mutate, save; no schema or migration machinery to maintain.
Consistent with single-user, single-process usage where only one writer exists (README.md).
disadvantages: Every change rewrites the whole file, so a crash mid-write can corrupt or lose the entire collection unless an atomic write pattern (temp file plus rename) is implemented carefully.
All notes are loaded into memory on every invocation, and every search or filter is executed in Python over the full collection.
No partial updates, transactions, or indexes; the approach does not extend well if query needs grow.
assumptions: The note collection stays small enough to load into memory comfortably.
Notes have a simple structure that maps cleanly to JSON objects and lists.
The CLI remains the only writer of the file, as the README states.

alternatives.name: SQLite database file
alternatives.description: Store notes as rows in a single SQLite database file (for example notes.db) accessed through the standard-library `sqlite3` module.
advantages: Transactional writes: an interrupted or crashed change does not leave the data half-updated or corrupt.
Supports indexed search, filtering, and ordering through SQL as the note collection grows.
`sqlite3` ships in the Python standard library, so the project keeps zero third-party runtime dependencies.
Data lives in one copyable file in a documented format with wide tooling support.
disadvantages: The data file is binary, so users cannot read or edit it in a plain text editor and must use SQLite tooling to inspect it.
Requires defining a table schema, writing SQL, and handling schema changes if note fields evolve.
More code and concepts (schema, queries, migration) than the current placeholder codebase has any use for yet.
assumptions: The `sqlite3` module is present in the Python builds users run notes-cli with (standard in CPython, omitted in some alternative interpreters).
Notes will eventually benefit from structured querying by metadata such as tags or dates.
Because only one process writes at a time (README.md), SQLite is used here for crash safety rather than multi-process coordination.

alternatives.name: One plain-text file per note
alternatives.description: Store each note as its own plain-text or Markdown file inside a notes directory, with metadata in a small header or front-matter block.
advantages: Maximally accessible outside the CLI: users can read, edit, grep, and version individual notes with any editor or git.
Each note is an independent file, so a bad write or corruption affects at most that one note.
Standard-library file I/O only; no third-party dependencies.
Notes remain usable entirely without the CLI, which suits a personal note-taking tool.
disadvantages: Cross-note queries such as search by tag or date require scanning and parsing every file, which grows slower as the collection grows.
Metadata stored in headers or front matter must be parsed and validated by hand-written code, which is easy to make inconsistent.
Filename and identifier management (uniqueness, renames, filesystem encoding limits) must be implemented manually.
assumptions: Users value direct access to note files outside the CLI.
Collection size and query needs stay modest.
A hand-rolled metadata convention is acceptable for this project.

criteria.name: Fit for an offline single-user CLI
rubric: Requires network services or a server, conflicting with the offline requirement
Works offline but adds operational overhead unsuited to a single-user CLI
Works fully offline on local files and matches single-user, single-process use

criteria.name: Data integrity on crash or partial write
rubric: A crash mid-write can corrupt or destroy the entire collection
A crash mid-write can affect at most a single note
Transactional writes guarantee the data is never left half-updated

criteria.name: Search and query as the collection grows
rubric: Every query scans and parses all notes in Python
Content can be searched with plain-text tools but metadata queries still require parsing every note
Indexed queries over metadata and content are supported by the store

criteria.name: Implementation effort for the current milestone
rubric: Requires building and maintaining significant infrastructure before notes can be saved
Requires moderate extra code such as a schema, migrations, or metadata conventions
Straightforward to implement with a small amount of code

criteria.name: Dependency footprint
rubric: Adds third-party runtime dependencies to a project that currently has none
Uses only the Python standard library, preserving the zero-dependency state

criteria.name: User access to data outside the CLI
rubric: Binary format that requires special tooling to read or edit
Plain-text format the user can read, edit, back up, and version with standard tools
